related_questions.question: Should I go to the hospital if my blood pressure is 140 over 90?

text_blocks.snippet: A blood pressure reading of 140/90 mmHg, while considered Stage 2 hypertension, doesn't automatically necessitate a trip to the hospital. It's advisable to monitor the reading and consult with a healthcare professional for personalized guidance. If the reading is consistently high (over several readings) or accompanied by symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, or stroke-like symptoms, then immediate medical attention is crucial, according to the Mayo Clinic.
snippet_highlighted_words: doesn't automatically necessitate a trip to the hospital

list.snippet: Normal: 120/80 mmHg or lower.
Elevated: 120-129/80 mmHg.
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130-139/80-89 mmHg.
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140/90 mmHg or higher.
Hypertensive Crisis: 180/120 mmHg or higher.

text_blocks.snippet: When to Seek Immediate Medical Care:

list.title: Hypertensive Crisis:
list.snippet: If your blood pressure reaches 180/120 mmHg or higher, and you experience symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, or stroke-like symptoms (weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking), it's crucial to call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room immediately, says www.heart.org.

list.title: Severe Symptoms:
list.snippet: Even without a hypertensive crisis reading, if you experience chest pain, severe headache, shortness of breath, or other concerning symptoms, seek immediate medical attention.

list.title: Repeated High Readings:
list.snippet: If you consistently get readings of 140/90 mmHg or higher over multiple readings and are concerned, consult your doctor promptly, according to GoodRx.

text_blocks.snippet: When to See Your Doctor Soon:

list.snippet: If your blood pressure is consistently in the Stage 2 hypertension range (140/90 mmHg or higher), even without symptoms, schedule an appointment with your doctor to discuss management and treatment options.
Your doctor can assess your overall health, determine the cause of your high blood pressure, and recommend appropriate lifestyle changes and/or medications.

text_blocks.snippet: What to Do in the Meantime:

list.title: Relax and Recheck:
list.snippet: If you're not experiencing any symptoms, try relaxing for a few minutes and recheck your blood pressure. Sometimes, a high reading can be due to stress or anxiety.

list.title: Monitor Your Blood Pressure:
list.snippet: Keep a record of your blood pressure readings, including the date and time, to share with your doctor.

list.title: Follow Your Doctor's Advice:
list.snippet: If you're already taking medication for high blood pressure, continue to follow your doctor's instructions.

text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major risk factor for stroke. It's the most important modifiable risk factor, meaning it's something you can control to reduce your risk. High blood pressure can damage blood vessels in the brain, making them prone to blockages (ischemic stroke) or rupture (hemorrhagic stroke).
snippet_highlighted_words: High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major risk factor for stroke

text_blocks.snippet: How High Blood Pressure Leads to Stroke:

list.title: Damaged Arteries:
list.snippet: High blood pressure can weaken and damage the arteries in the brain, making them more susceptible to blockages or ruptures.

list.title: Blood Clots:
list.snippet: High blood pressure can contribute to the formation of blood clots, which can block blood flow to the brain and cause an ischemic stroke.

list.title: Weakened Vessels:
list.snippet: Over time, high blood pressure can weaken blood vessel walls, increasing the risk of a hemorrhagic stroke (bleeding in the brain).

list.title: Increased Risk:
list.snippet: People with high blood pressure are significantly more likely to have a stroke than those with normal blood pressure.

list.title: Emergency Threshold:
list.snippet: Blood pressure readings of 180/120 mmHg or higher are considered stroke-level and require immediate medical attention.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: High blood pressure can manifest in various ways, including severe headaches, dizziness, vision problems, nosebleeds, and facial flushing.

list.title: Immediate Action:
list.snippet: If you experience these symptoms, especially with a blood pressure reading at or above 180/120 mmHg, call 911 immediately.

list.title: Blood Pressure Management:
list.snippet: Controlling high blood pressure is crucial for stroke prevention.

list.title: Lifestyle Changes:
list.snippet: Adopting a healthy lifestyle, including a balanced diet, regular exercise, and stress management, can help lower blood pressure.

list.title: Medication:
list.snippet: If lifestyle changes are not enough, medication may be necessary to manage blood pressure effectively.

list.title: Regular Checkups:
list.snippet: Regular checkups with your doctor can help monitor your blood pressure and identify any potential issues early on.
